IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail

“I. Kay Khosraw possessed the Grail, the mirror of the universe. Whatever his heart desired, he could contemplate in that Grail. Through it he learned of the invisible worlds; within it he surveyed the whole of existence.

“II. This Grail was enclosed in a leather scabbard, shaped on a lathe and fitted with ten joints. Whenever Kay Khosraw wished to learn some further mystery of the Invisible, he set this scabbard turning again (to undo it). When he had loosened every bond, the Grail was no longer visible. But when the turning bound all the joints together once more, the Grail appeared.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-01052

“III. At the spring equinox, Kay Khosraw held the Grail directly facing the Sun. When the star’s radiance struck the Grail, all the lines and impressions of all the worlds could be contemplated there, made manifest.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-01053

“When the Earth is spread out flat, casts forth what it contains and remains empty, when it listens to its Lord and becomes worthy of Him—then you, O human being, you who strive on your way towards your Lord, behold, you meet Him (84:3–5). — Nothing hidden within you will remain concealed (69:18). — Every soul will know what it has sent ahead of itself and what it has left behind (82:5).
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-01054

“IV. When I heard my master tell the Tale of the Grail of Jam, I myself became the Grail of Jam, the mirror of the universe. Let my own Grail, the mirror of the universe, be drawn from its sheath; This buried Grail is the burning Flame that feeds upon our death.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-01055

In this brief and astonishing “Tale of the Grail,” all the conditions we have examined in the preceding pages are enacted, brought together, and confirmed. The content of the doctrine that leads towards self-knowledge flowers into the image of Kay Khosraw’s Grail, at once a real object and a real event. The Unsayable which Eastern Theosophy has struggled to express is accomplished as the “return to the East.” The event becomes the hidden meaning of doctrine, and the fulfilment of that hidden meaning. At the same time, the tale expresses it beneath the outward appearance of a sensus litteralis.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-01056

Yet the hidden meaning of this “literal sense” is not a return to the theoretical certainty of the doctrine that explains what the “East” is. It lies on the higher level where doctrine, having become event, brings the initiate to awareness of the Event whose very place of occurrence is his own person: “I was—I became—the Grail of Jam, the mirror of the universe.” The Grail is a real object, but real in the way that objects of the supersensible world are real. It is a real event, although it does not occur in our world and breaks the course of its history.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-01057

Indeed, it is so real that it is never “superseded,” because it is always waiting to “take place.” What makes the Word true is not that it belonged to “its own time,” as historical consciousness understands the phrase, but that it becomes the time of every faithful initiate in whom the Event is accomplished.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-01058

Thus the ta’wil practised by Suhrawardi in his Tale of the Grail and his other mystical stories is in perfect accord with his own ta’wil of the Holy Book. He sets out its rule as follows: “Recite the Quran in ecstasy (wajd), with inward emotion and subtle reflection. Recite the Quran as though it had been revealed for your own case alone.” This brings us back to the “phenomenon of the Holy Book,” as expressed in the saying of the Fifth Imam, Muhammad al-Baqir (see Book I above). If the Quranic verses had meaning only in relation to the circumstances and people for whom they were revealed, the entire Quran would have been dead long ago!
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-01059
But ta’wil, the interpretation that makes it the hikayat, the story of each believer who recites it in Suhrawardi’s manner, keeps it alive “until the Day of Resurrection.”
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-01060

The two mystical tales by Suhrawardi which we shall now translate will offer further examples. In The Tale of the Western Exile, the stages of the exile’s “return journey” are marked by Quranic verses which ta’wil applies to the mystic’s personal situation. These verses mark the successive stages of his spiritual state until he reaches the “East,” the “celestial pole.” At the conclusion we shall encounter a figure recognisable as the one whom Suhrawardi’s Hermeticism has already introduced to us as “Perfect Nature.” Before that, we shall read The Tale of the Crimson Archangel.
IV. The Light of Glory and the Holy Grail
passage-en-01061

At two decisive moments in the initiation the archangel gives his earthly companion, two episodes from the Iranian mystical epic will enter the story. Once more we shall see that the heroic adventure finds its fulfilment in the mystical adventure, which enacts its “Eastern” destiny. This is how Suhrawardi proceeds throughout his Eastern Theosophy: he leads the sages of ancient Persia forward into Islam and back to the “Eastern Source,” bringing forth the Ishraqiyun, the Neoplatonists of Islamic Persia, as the spiritual heirs of the Khosrawaniyun of ancient Persia.

1. The Purpose of the Tale
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01063

The “Tale of the Grail” has just shown us, in living action, the “Eastern” goal of the “Eastern theosophy”—the wisdom of the spiritual East. We have seen at work the threefold unity implied by the hikâyat, the mystical recital: the person telling the tale, the heroic story being told, and the hero whose deeds are retold merge into a single reality, different in each individual case.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01064

The ishrâqî mystic, a seeker of illumination, speaks in the first person as a khosrawânî, a sage of ancient Iran; he himself is the Grail of Kay Khosrow. In the same movement, the Ishrâqîyûn (the Illuminationists) become the living hikâyat of the Khosrawânîyûn, the sages of ancient Iran. Through them, the deeds of their predecessors are enacted again, made present even in Islamic Persia, by means of ta’wîl, the spiritual interpretation whose secret is preserved and extended by the inner tradition of Islam.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01065

When the Grail is unveiled—and its true identity is disclosed—the Eastern adventure reaches its end in an anticipation of the soul’s final departure, its exitus. It fulfils the Prophet of Islam’s injunction: “Learn to die spiritually before physical death overtakes you.” The fear and darkness of ignorance that make us dread death are now dispelled. The initiate knows that he is going home, and knows the way. “The indescribable has become real.” What had not yet been accomplished has happened; it has become an event, an accomplished fact.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01066
For an Illuminationist, this indescribable reality is precisely what the Book of Eastern Theosophy attempts to describe, along with the major works that prepare the way for it.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01067

Yet Suhrawardi and the Illuminationists said repeatedly that reading books is not enough to make one a member of the family of the “hieratic” sages, those who have themselves attained spiritual knowledge. Books can set the reader on the path and guide him toward fulfilment, but in themselves they remain no more than a possibility.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01068

One must acquire the ability, as a settled habit, to slip out of the physical senses as though taking off a garment—the leather sheath that concealed the Grail of Kay Khosrow—and enter the “eighth clime,” the Middle Orient of the spirit, the mundus imaginalis, or imaginal world, which stands at the threshold of the greater spiritual Easts. To a historian accustomed to the usual categories of the outward history of religions, what seems inconceivable may be the sudden, compelling reappearance, at the heart of the Sufism of Islamic Persia, of figures from the Zoroastrian tradition of ancient Persia.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01069

Yet here that apparent impossibility has become a spiritual fact, embodied and made intelligible in the person of the Shaykh al-Ishrâq, the Master of Illumination. Before him, we could certainly search for traces that would establish a passage and continuity between the two Persias. Such traces are plentiful, but they can always be disputed, as traces are disputed when the person who left them is no longer present. From the time of the Master of Illumination onward, we are no longer dealing merely with remnants to be collected. We confront the compelling presence of a spiritual event that will itself leave its mark on everything that follows: the Illuminationist tradition of Islamic Iran.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01070

The figure of Kay Khosrow, the king who attains ecstasy, dominates the spiritual horizon of ancient Iran as Suhrawardi sees it. We already know the principle that governs our master’s practice of ta’wîl: “Recite the Quran as though it had been revealed for your own case alone.” His “case” is that of a seeker of spiritual knowledge whose vision opens onto many spiritual universes. They hold the secret of his own story, because it is from them that he came, and to them that he returns. His story is a metahistory: it breaks free of the straight line imposed by outward history, for neither its origin nor its future has its place on that level of reality.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01071

To become contemporary with that past and that future—to meet them together in the present—requires a critical understanding of time. Such an understanding would later be developed by other thinkers, notably, as we have mentioned, the great Shia philosopher Qazi Sa'id Qommi.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01072

Suhrawardi could apply this principle of interpretation not only when reciting the Quran but also when reading the book that, for Islamic Persia, serves almost as a Bible of ancient Iran’s heroic deeds: Ferdowsi’s tenth-century Shâh-Nâmeh, the Book of Kings.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01073

We can imagine him reading the Shâh-Nâmeh as we read the Bible, or as he himself read the Quran: as though it had been written for his own case alone. We have just recalled what that case involves. Read in this way, the Shâh-Nâmeh could become the history—or rather the metahistory—of the soul as it lives in the heart of the spiritual seeker.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01074

Suhrawardi could therefore perceive, woven into the very fabric of the Shâh-Nâmeh, the whole history of the soul and its world. This is the level on which the poem becomes readable once we keep in mind the fullness of being and all its worlds. It is much as the distinguished Neoplatonist Proclus knew how to read the story of mysterious Atlantis: as a true history and, at the same time, as the “image of a certain reality existing within the Whole.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01075

A commentary on the Shâh-Nâmeh along these lines would be fascinating. It would show the poem interpreted in a way comparable to the reading of Homer’s Odyssey in Hellenistic religious devotion. Unfortunately, apart from the exceptional figure of Kay Khosrow, the Master of Illumination has left us indications of a spiritual interpretation for only three other heroes of the Shâh-Nâmeh: Zal, Rostam, and Esfandiyar. Yet those indications are of enormous significance.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01076

We shall see the meaning of these three figures emerge at the heart of the work translated here as the “Tale of the Crimson Archangel.” This is precisely why, having to choose among Suhrawardi’s mystical tales, we gave this one precedence over the others.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01077

Following the example of Kay Khosrow, this tale allows us to understand particularly well how Suhrawardi’s spiritual interpretation discovers the Eastern fulfilment of the heroic epic: the history of the soul encoded within it. It shows how the Iranian heroic epic reaches its resolution as a mystical adventure. This is certainly not a matter of abstract speculation or a table of correspondences from which one can produce automatic translations of one thing into another.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01078

The meaning of Zal’s story and of Rostam’s is suggested to us only as something learned in “conversation with the Angel.” That conversation, too, takes place “between Heaven and Earth.” In following the outline of the Shâh-Nâmeh, the story of the soul awakened to spiritual knowledge descending into this world and its ascent in an ecstatic exitus, made possible by the powers of the higher worlds, is distributed between the figures of Zal and Esfandiyar.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01079

But this arrangement is not something whose meaning can be proved by logical argument. The certainty disclosed by spiritual interpretation belongs to a level beyond both the senses’ perception of the heroes’ outward exploits and the grasp of ordinary reason.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01080
Indeed, the hidden meaning of the stories of Zal and Rostam is revealed only in enigmatic phrases, almost in passing.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01081

Yet their connection with the mystical bird Simorgh tells us that this is the secret of the whole tale. Understanding that secret determines whether the Angel’s disciple can answer the Angel’s veiled challenge: “If you are Khezr, you too can pass through.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01082

Through its paired episodes concerning Zal and Esfandiyar, the “Tale of the Crimson Archangel” is thus immediately linked to the Iranian heroic epic, now destined to find its fulfilment as a mystical epic.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01083

Another of the Master of Illumination’s tales, by contrast, is more directly connected through its imagery with ancient gnosis and Hermeticism: the “Tale of the Western Exile.” This is the second tale we have chosen to translate here. We chose the pair not only because together they bring to life the dominant elements of Eastern theosophy—Neoplatonically interpreted Zoroastrianism and Hermeticism—but also because the two tales have a special relationship to one another. They stand in much the same relation as two works in Avicenna’s cycle of visionary tales: the “Tale of Hayy ibn Yaqzan” and the “Tale of the Bird.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01084

The first describes the terrain; it maps the universes that the mystic must cross to escape the “cosmic crypt.” The “Tale of the Bird” is the actual flight, carrying the pilgrim all the way to the end of his spiritual ascent. In just this way, the two tales of Suhrawardi translated here complete and answer one another, forming a single whole.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01085

We said earlier that someone gifted with the vision can see the “eighth clime,” but cannot show it to someone else—not even point out the landmarks of the way in any effective manner. Only an Angel can attempt to do that. The “Tale of the Crimson Archangel” shows the direction, indicates the road, and hints at how one may “pass through,” culminating in the final invitation: “If you are Khezr…” The “Tale of the Western Exile,” for its part, returns to the very beginning, as the first tale does.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01086

But the exile then answers the invitation he has received: he sets out. His road is full of adventures, until at last he reaches the “Emerald Rock.” He must come back, for until the final exitus every ecstasy is fleeting.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01087

But at least he now knows the road he himself must travel. He tries, in turn, to indicate its stages. He does so, however, by encoding them in Quranic verses that must be deciphered with the aid of ta’wîl. And to use that key of interpretation, one must oneself set out upon the road.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01088

Here again we must avoid a misunderstanding. The few indications we give in our introductions to these tales are justified only if we remember what was said earlier (Chapter IV, section 4) about this kind of explanation. It would be a paradox—indeed an illusion—to suppose that one had explained the meaning of a mystical or initiatory tale by reducing the events it recounts or evokes to a set of theoretical doctrines, however sublime those doctrines might be. For the very purpose of the tale, as a mystical tale, is to pass beyond them. Suhrawardi’s earliest commentators, writing in Arabic or Persian, certainly tried to provide the keys to his tales by proceeding in just this way.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01089

Yet when we have finished reading their explanations, we see that, if we stopped there, we would have missed everything that makes the tale a drama. Taken instead as guides to orientation, their commentaries are extremely useful. They are ductus lectionis, guides to reading, and nothing more. If they alone could give us the “inner meaning” of an action whose narrative form supplied merely its “literal meaning,” Suhrawardi would have had no reason to write his cycle of tales at all. He wrote them because his great teaching treatises, and the form he had adopted in those works, still fell short of what he needed to say.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01090

What he needed to express was no longer only the coherent body of theosophical teaching, but that same teaching transformed into an event of his own soul. Each stage of the doctrine became a stage of the journey: a state actually lived and realized by a soul making, in reality, the pilgrimage described by the teaching. Exposition became story. The story, then, is not the starting point from which the doctrine is derived.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01091

Nor does it speak of events taking place in our phenomenal world, the world of outward history. It is already the elevation of the doctrine to the level of events occurring in the world of the Soul, the malakût. This is why, from the standpoint of teaching, the doctrine may be called the tale’s inner or esoteric meaning; yet from the standpoint of spiritual realization, it is the tale that reveals the inner meaning of the doctrine.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01092

Whenever we refer to a point of cosmology, psychology, or angelology to “clarify” a particular phase of the narrated event, we must not forget that the cosmological theory, for example, is not in itself the tale’s esoteric meaning. It becomes that meaning only when it is raised to the level of the tale and transformed by it into an event. Then, indeed, the theory is the tale’s meaning, precisely because the tale is the theory’s happening, its fulfilment. This “circle of interpretation” simply reflects Suhrawardi’s fundamental conviction: philosophy that does not culminate in mystical experience, in a “hieratic” ascent, is barren and meaningless. Conversely, mystical experience without prior philosophical training runs a serious risk of going astray.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01093
But brought together, the two attain a level higher than either could reach on its own.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01094

We have stressed this point before (Chapter IV, section 4, levels A, B, and C), because it seems to us that the most serious misunderstandings about interpretation lie hidden here. The “Tale of the Western Exile” will provide a further, exact confirmation. In that tale, particular stages of the “return” are represented by particular Quranic verses. The journey of return is therefore the esoteric meaning of those verses.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01095

It follows that the fulfilment of the event cannot be sought in the mere words of the Quranic verse, but in what those words mean when they are lived and realized—made present again through action, in accordance with Suhrawardi’s interpretation and that of the Fifth Imam. The meanings of the Quranic verses then unfold across several levels of the universe.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01096

At each level, the literal meaning proper to that level is true and is at the same time a spiritual meaning; that literal-and-spiritual meaning is, in turn, the esoteric meaning relative to the level immediately below it. The visionary landscapes that open before the soul in the mundus imaginalis, and the figures who appear within them, are therefore real with the reality proper to supersensible beings.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01097
But this reality is far more than the reality of a mere literal narrative whose esoteric meaning would be supplied by theoretical doctrine.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01098

We can now understand why a theosophy expressed through dramatic action passes beyond the level at which it could, or should, furnish the “dialectical proofs” available to theoretical reason. Its grounds of certainty and its proofs are essentially those of directly tasted wisdom: dhawq, related here to the Latin sapere, knowledge that actually savours what it knows. And this knowing, a spiritual knowledge that saves, is inseparable from the movement of faith; it is that movement itself.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01099

We can only be astonished by certain sweeping, categorical claims made today against gnosis—for instance, the assertion that it tries to provide faith with a second set of truths carrying the same kind of certainty as the exact sciences. Such a claim betrays a very limited acquaintance with gnosis. We have expressly rejected any idea of knowledge running alongside faith as a duplicate of it.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01100

But if one begins by separating pistis (îmân, fides), faith, from gnôsis (’irfân), spiritual knowledge, one will obviously never succeed in bringing them together again in the unity of theosophia (hikmat ilâhîya), divine wisdom.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01101

Let us now use these principles to examine the themes of the “Tale of the Crimson Archangel.” The tale begins with an important prologue. At its close, seven themes are announced, which the Angel will then develop in the teaching through which he initiates his disciple.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
en-book-2-ch-5-s2
2. The Prologue to the Tale
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01102
The prologue itself unfolds in several stages.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01103

a) A question put to the author by a friend provides the opening: the pre-existence of the soul. Here the reader will recall the magnificent image in Plato’s Phaedrus of souls following the gods in a heavenly procession, and of the fall of some among them. The soul’s wings naturally suggest the form of a bird.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01104

Hence the first motif: the “language of the birds” (Mantiq al-tayr). The Quran speaks of this language (27:16), saying that Solomon, as a prophet, had received the gift of understanding it. To understand the language of birds is to understand the language of all created beings as they speak through their very existence. Each thing is then alive and has a voice; each reveals its secret. To understand that language is to possess the key to symbols. This precious gift is therefore associated with the state of the soul before its fall into our world.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01105

Moreover, Mantiq al-Tayr, The Language of the Birds, is the title of one of the best-known Persian mystical epics, by Farid al-Din Attar (twelfth century), whose culmination is the episode of Simorgh. We have already encountered that name here, and shall meet it again, for Simorgh is of great importance in Suhrawardi’s tales.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01106

b) The soul’s pre-existence leads naturally to the next theme: its fall into captivity. We hear of the hunters called “Decree and Destiny, spreading the net of predestination.” Proclus, too, speaks of hunters, those who “together with the daimones, pursue souls and imprison them in bodies.” More immediately, Suhrawardi’s theme here closely resembles Avicenna’s visionary tales.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01107

The “Tale of the Bird,” originally written in Arabic by Avicenna and translated into Persian by Suhrawardi, begins in a similar way. It speaks of searching for a friend to whom one might entrust a secret, and makes a moving appeal to the “Brothers of Truth.” Then the narrative begins: “When the hunters caught sight of us, they gave a whistle so pleasing that it lured us into uncertainty […] and suddenly we fell into the nets.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01108

Suhrawardi develops the same theme in the mystical rhapsody called “The Language of the Ants,” from which we earlier drew his “Tale of the Grail.” Elsewhere in that work, in its eighth chapter, he returns to the image of a captive bird. This time it is not a falcon, but a bird whose plumage reflects the colours of paradise: a peacock. “A king had a garden that was never, in any of the four seasons, without sweet herbs, greenery, and places of delight […]. Every joy the mind could conceive, every beauty the imagination could picture, was present in that garden.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01109

“Moreover, a flock of peacocks of the utmost grace, beauty, and delicacy had settled there, and the garden had become their homeland. One day the king took a peacock from among them and ordered it to be sewn inside a skin, so that none of the colours of its plumage remained visible and, try as it might, it could no longer see its own beauty […]. The peacock lost all memory of itself; it forgot the king, the garden, and the other peacocks.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01110

Thereafter the bird’s whole horizon was reduced to the slit in a little basket through which food was passed to it, “and the conviction took root in its heart that no country could be larger than the bottom of the basket.” Once again, the peacock sewn into a covering of skin recalls the Grail buried inside its leather sheath. For the Grail to appear, or for the bird’s true form to become visible, each must be freed from the covering that conceals it.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01111

In either case, its reappearance means reappearing in its own world, the world from which it descended only to be hidden here under an enclosing skin. To become visible again in its own world is to become invisible to this one. This is one of the ruling themes of Illuminationist gnosis, and indeed of spiritual gnosis in general.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01112
We shall encounter another version at the beginning of the “Tale of the Western Exile.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01113

c) Captivity and the fall are followed by escape. This theme recurs in the other mystical tales. Each time, the author evokes a state in which the senses are “bound,” thereby releasing the person from subjection to the world of sensory perception. The state can be represented by “night”: when night conceals the world of the senses, the soul’s powers of higher understanding awaken. It is the moment when the Grail is drawn out of its covering and hidden from the sight of this world.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01114

The initiate is not a schizophrenic; he knows perfectly well that he is between two worlds, that his liberation is not yet complete. The bird in our tale says: “Struggling all the while with my bonds, I finally made my way into the desert.” The same detail appears in Avicenna’s “Tale of the Bird.” The “desert,” the solitary open country—evoking the lonely expanses of the Iranian plateau, where infinite variety is gathered into a few essential tones—is always the first place reached by the soul escaping the turmoil of the outer world’s perceptions.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01115
Another tale, the “Epistle on the State of Childhood,” likewise opens in the desert.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01116

d) The escape into the desert leads immediately to the encounter with the Angel. The prologue to another tale, “The Rustling of Gabriel’s Wings,” already shows us the Child—the heavenly human being—freed from the bonds imposed on the children of Earth. These bonds are the limitations of knowledge gained through the senses, which keep earthly human beings in servitude, sunk in the sleep of their soul’s death. It is therefore night for the senses.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01117

The active Imagination is left entirely free to perceive the realities of the world belonging to it, the mundus imaginalis, which begins at the summit of Mount Qaf. At the coming of the mystical dawn, the hour of Ishrâq or illumination, the visionary opens the door of the khângâh, the Sufi lodge, leading out into the countryside. In other words, at the threshold of his innermost awareness, his “transconsciousness,” he opens the secret door onto an unexplored wilderness.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01118

Crossing it will take him to the country from which he came into this world. “It was a night when … darkness … had spread to the furthest limits of the lower world … I took a torch in my hand … and walked until daybreak … I closed the door that led toward the town … I wanted to open the door that led into the countryside … I saw ten Sages with radiant faces …” These Sages stand in a hierarchy of ranks. Their beauty fills the visionary with amazement. He approaches the nearest with reverent awe, and his initiation begins.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01119

This is not an initiation into cosmology; Suhrawardi had already set out his cosmology in his major works. It is an initiation into the angelology that gives cosmology its inner meaning. There are three orders of Angels: the Karûbiyûn, the Cherubim or cherubic Intelligences, who are the greater Logoi, the greater divine Words; the intermediate Logoi or Words, the heavenly Souls that move the Spheres; and finally the lesser Logoi or Words, human beings, who are potentially angels or demons.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01120

Here, again, the angelology is not a matter of theory but of an event. The visionary really does find himself, in actu, before the one among the greater Words who stands closest to him. Who is this being? The text leaves no doubt: Gabriel, or the Holy Spirit, the Tenth Intelligence in the angelic hierarchy, the Angel of humanity.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01121

To human beings, he is the interpreter of the higher worlds. Without him, those worlds, lying beyond the limits of human perception, would have nothing to offer but eternal silence. The relationship of this Angel with each individual human being takes a personal form: that Perfect Nature to which Suhrawardi dedicated one of his most beautiful psalms (see above, p. 138). In the end it is this Perfect Nature that undertakes the initiation, for it sometimes speaks of Gabriel in the third person. Gabriel the Archangel has two wings.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01122

The right wing is pure, absolute light; across the left lies a shadowy mark, like the reddish darkening that veils the face of the moon as it rises full. The world of illusion, the world of becoming or genesis, is a shadow cast by Gabriel’s left wing; from his right wing emanate the souls of light. With the revelation of the “heavenly Self,” the horizon of a human existence beyond ordinary existence opens. When the “day” of sensory perceptions and their certainties rises once more, the vision ends.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01123

Keep in mind this brief account of the prologue Suhrawardi placed at the beginning of “The Rustling of Gabriel’s Wings.” In the “Tale of the Crimson Archangel,” the soul is in the same circumstances and encounters the same Figure, recognizable by the same features. No sooner has the visionary entered the desert than he sees a mysterious person approaching, a youth whose appearance enchants him. And yet, as he learns, this young man is “the eldest of the Creator’s children.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01124

To grasp exactly what this statement means, we must recall the distinction we have already encountered between the “world of the Divine Command” (’âlam al-Amr), which comprises the jabarût and malakût, and the “world of created beings” (’âlam al-khalq), embracing the whole world of becoming, to which human beings presently belong. As the “Angel of humanity” (Rabb al-nû’ al-insânî), Gabriel can call himself the “eldest” of the Creator’s children.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01125

The distinguishing feature of this vision is its red or glowing crimson colour. That colour gives the tale its title, and makes the title difficult to translate in a way that speaks for itself. The Persian title is ’Aql-e sorkh. The word ’aql (plural ’oqûl) is the traditional name for the cherubic Intelligences, whose ten hierarchical ranks we have just recalled.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01126

In the Latin Avicennian tradition, these are the Angeli intellectuales, the intellectual Angels, while the Angeli caelestes, the heavenly Angels, form the intermediate hierarchy of Souls that move the Spheres. The last of the cherubic Intelligences is Gabriel, the Holy Spirit, the Angel of knowledge and revelation for humanity, the philosophers’ Active Intelligence, the Madonna Intelligenza of the Faithful of Love in Dante’s circle. Sorkh means “red.” We feared that translating the title simply as “The Red Intelligence” would mislead readers, if indeed it conveyed anything to them.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01127

Moreover, when the Angel explains his “colour” to the disciple, he speaks of the purple-red glow of twilight. Since the ’oqûl, the Intelligences, are also called archangels, the title suggested itself at once: Tale of the Crimson Archangel. The Angel’s explanation tells us that this colour, crimson red, comes from the mingling of light and darkness, of white and black. This is precisely what the symbolism of Gabriel’s “two wings,” recalled above, is meant to convey. From the standpoint of our physics, the explanation may seem surprising; if we wished to account for it experimentally, we might think of a ray of light passing through stained glass.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01128

But an optical phenomenon is not what matters here. The colour has, above all, a meaning beyond the senses and a symbolic function. The closer a being is to the source of being, the more it tends toward whiteness; the closer it comes to the world of genesis, the more it tends toward black.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01129

This striking feature of Suhrawardi’s visionary tales must therefore be understood in relation to the symbolism of colours in Islamic theosophy. The theme has so far received very little study. It is initially organized around the image of the Throne, which plays a role in Islamic gnosis comparable to that of the Merkabah, the divine chariot-throne, in Jewish Kabbalah.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01130

The Throne’s four “pillars,” representing the foundations of being, correspond to the four archangels—Seraphiel, Michael, Gabriel, and Azrael—each appearing in a colour of his own. The arrangement varies somewhat from one author to another. Qazi Sa'id Qommi, in particular, gave a remarkable analysis of the metaphysical meaning of the gradual “diminution” of white light: it passes through yellow, red, and green as it descends toward the world of Darkness. We cannot pursue the subject further here.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01131

Let us at least note how the same theme appears in the work of several other great Iranian spiritual masters. In the visions of Najm al-Din Kubra (d. 618/1221), among the perceived lights that lie beyond the senses—the spiritual aura—a glowing crimson announces the Angel-Intelligence in a double form: in the great world, the macrocosm, as the Angel-Logos, a manifestation of the Inaccessible; and in the small world, the microcosm, as the heart, a consciousness made of light. Later, in Book IV, we shall encounter Semnani (d. 736/1336) and his account of the seven subtle organs or sheaths (latîfa) that constitute the subtle body of mystical physiology.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01132

Each makes itself known to the mystic’s supersensible perception by a particular colour, and each is represented by a prophet. The latîfa corresponding to the heart—the “Abraham of your being”—is red. We should also recall the predominance of red light in the visions of Ruzbihan of Shiraz (d. 606/1209), discussed in Book III. “One night I saw something enveloping the heavens. It was a sparkling red light. I asked: What is this? I was told: It is the mantle of magnificence.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01133

Finally, in the last century, Shaykh Muhammad Karim Khan Kermani, the second successor of Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i (see Book VI below), composed, among many other works, a long treatise on the colour red. He considered it from its optical appearance, essence, and nature through to its symbolic and mystical meanings.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01134

Of these examples, and others we could add, the essential point to retain is the connection between the heart as the dwelling place of knowledge and Gabriel as the Angel who mediates that knowledge. Here, as in similar tales by Suhrawardi, the Angel performs the same function as Poimandres in the first treatise of the Corpus Hermeticum. The Nous, the Intelligence, appears to Hermes as his initiator. We have already traced this figure in Suhrawardi’s “Perfect Nature” and in the Illuminationist tradition.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01135

An angel who serves as the human being’s shepherd (poimên) also appears in The Shepherd of Hermas, that delightful little book so rich in symbolic visions, which for a time formed part of the canonical Scriptures. Hermas’s “shepherd” is the angel personally entrusted with his care. In each instance, the personal angel—the Hermetic “Perfect Nature”—appears under similar circumstances. Just as Hermas’s angel is sent by the glorious Angel, the “Most Holy Angel,” whom the context suggests is Michael the Archangel, so the Perfect Nature expresses for the Illuminationist initiate his own individually distinct relationship with the Angel of humanity.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01136

We should also remember that the great Iranian poet Hakim Sana'i of Herat (d. 545/1150), who died a few years before Suhrawardi’s birth, had already written a poem called “The Journey of Souls to the Place of Their Return,” in the form of a first-person narrative. It describes a journey through the Neoplatonic cosmos under the guidance of the Active Intelligence, appearing as a personal angel or guide. Even so, Suhrawardi’s initiatory tales in prose remain unique in Persian literature.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01137

Finally, his tales ought to be considered alongside the theory of spiritual knowledge developed in Shia teaching on prophecy, based on the words of the holy Imams. This theory distinguishes between actually seeing an Angel while awake, seeing an Angel in a dream or intermediate state, and merely hearing the Angel’s voice without a vision. According to these distinctions, it establishes degrees of sacred knowledge, from prophetic revelation to mystical inspiration (see Book I above). We have, indeed, already seen that the accusation brought against Suhrawardi at his trial was directed at the understanding of prophecy implicit in his entire teaching.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01138

e) Once the disciple has identified the Angel, he wants to know more: where does the Angel come from? From beyond Mount Qaf, he answers—from the place where he dwells and where his disciple, too, once dwelt, before falling captive into this world. The disciple has lost all memory of that home because his awareness is confined within the limits of the very world that holds him prisoner. The whole purpose of the initiatory tale is to teach him to recognize the stages of the journey that will carry the exile across Mount Qaf and out of the cosmic crypt.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01139

We have already said enough about Mount Qaf, the cosmic mountain, not to need another lengthy account. We know that at its summit, or in its heart, begins the “eighth clime”: the “Middle East,” the mundus imaginalis, the Earth of emerald cities, the “Land of No-Where” (Nâ-kojâ-Abâd). It is called “No-Where” because it lies beyond the spatial coordinates contained beneath the Sphere of Spheres. The Angel will point toward it only from afar, as if by a gesture. The pilgrim himself will enter it, for a moment, only at the end of the following tale.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01140

But before setting out, he must learn the stages of the road. These are what the Angel will reveal through the seven wonders he has observed in his ceaseless travels through the world. This perpetual wandering is also a feature of Hayy ibn Yaqzan in Avicenna’s tale of that name. Every human intelligence the Angel illuminates marks another stage of his journey. The very nature of the seven wonders, which will become the seven themes of the tale proper, makes clear what he means by endless travel: he goes from soul to soul, awakening each through his illumination from its torpor.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic

3. The Seven Themes of the Tale
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01141

I. The first of these “wonders” is Mount Qaf itself, which the Angel names first when he says where he comes from. We already know that this mountain belongs both to the cosmos and to the inner cosmos of the soul. Traditional accounts that speak of it in a literal sense agree in identifying it with the mountain range encircling the world, formerly known as Alborz (Elburz; in the Avesta, Haraiti Bareza). Geographically, that name now designates the mountains stretching across northern Iran.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01142

But visionary geography is not concerned with this measurable feature of the Earth’s terrain when it speaks of a mountain surrounding the world, and of the wondrous race inhabiting its cities. More precisely, this is a “cartography of vision,” a mapping that locates and names places according to the visionary experiences corresponding to them. At that level, the true meaning of Alborz appears in its “visionary calling.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01143

As the cosmic mountain surrounding our earthly world, Mount Qaf, or Alborz, is described by the Angel as actually consisting of eleven mountains. Their succession of peaks and valleys represents the nine heavenly Spheres—from the heaven of the Moon to the Sphere of Spheres—together with the spheres of the Elements: the cold region of the sphere of Water and the hot regions of the spheres of Air and Fire.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01144

The Angel’s listener is concerned above all with one question: how can he get out? How can he cross these mountains and finally reach the summit of Mount Qaf? The hardest task is to escape the first two mountains, representing the earthly human condition: bondage to the Elements, to the physical body composed of them, and to the kind of perception that this condition imposes.
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01145

The Angel proceeds through hints and veiled suggestions: “However far you travel, and however long you keep going, you will arrive once more at your point of departure.” This is because the spiritual person’s “place of return” (ma’âd) is also the place of his origin (mabdâ’). It is in no sense a matter of setting out from oneself only to arrive, quite simply, back at oneself. Between departure and return, a great event will have transformed everything. The self found up there at the summit of Mount Qaf is the higher self, the “self in the second person,” encountered face to face by the pilgrim in the “Tale of the Western Exile.”
V. “The Crimson Archangel” and the Iranian Mystical Epic
passage-en-01146

Consider closely the Angel’s understated lesson when the questioner proposes using great physical force to cross the mountains. If you pour a drop of balm into the hollow of your hand and hold your hand in the sun until it grows hot, the balm will pass through to the other side of your hand by virtue of its own natural power. The same symbol will return at the end of the tale: the one who has bathed in the Spring of Life, on emerging from its waters, has acquired the capacity that makes him like the drop of balm. Such a person is Khezr, and can pass through. It then takes only an instant to cross these mountains.
